title: Setting Multiple Priorities Lets Leaders Off the Hook
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership Field Note uses etymology to challenge the habit of naming many priorities. The word priority meant the first thing for five centuries and was only pluralized in the 20th century, which gave leaders a linguistic escape hatch from deciding what matters most. The piece argues that declaring five priorities, ten imperatives and a stack of KPIs is itself a decision, and usually the wrong one, because they all compete for the same finite time, attention and resources. It reframes the problem as a refusal to choose that is usually about protection: of stakeholder relationships, of the pressure to extract more results from a team, or of the accountability that comes with committing publicly. The remedy is to name a single priority, commit to it publicly and hold the line, while accepting that other work can still continue.
points: Pluralizing the word priority let leaders avoid the hardest choice in leadership, which is deciding what is most important.
Naming everything a priority is itself a decision, and it leaves nothing first because every item competes for the same limited resources.
Leaders who pluralize priorities are typically protecting stakeholder relationships, pushing a team to juggle more, or avoiding public accountability.
The diagnostic question for any leader with many priorities is what he or she is avoiding and losing by refusing to name one.
Elevating a single priority does not stop other work; it identifies where the lion's share of attention goes right now.
quotes: In many organizations, leaders proudly communicate five priorities, 10 strategic imperatives, eight critical success factors, and a host of KPIs and OKRs.
The problem is that naming everything a priority is itself a decision, and usually the wrong one.
When a leader says, “Everything is a priority,” then nothing comes first or is more important than anything else.
But the etymology suggests something else entirely. The real problem is a refusal to choose, and refusing to choose is usually about protection.
The question every leader who creates multiple priorities must ask is, “What am I avoiding and losing by refusing to name one?
Elevating a single priority doesn’t mean nothing else can or should take place. It simply highlights the one thing that must receive the lion’s share of the team’s attention and focus right now.
The word was singular for 500 years for a reason. One thing comes first, and everything else follows.
